# Behavioral Economics and Medication Adherence for Hypertension: A Randomized Clinical Trial

**Authors:** John A. Dodson; Samrachana Adhikari; Antoinette M. Schoenthaler; Daichi Shimbo; Adam N. Berman; Natalie Levy; Kathleen Hanley; Safiya Richardson; Ashwini Varghese; Yuchen Meng; Stephanie Pena; Stefany de Brito; Yasmin Gutierrez; Michelle Rojas; Victoria Rosado; Ekaterina Olkhinha; Andrea B. Troxel

**Affiliations:** 1NYU Grossman School of Medicine, New York, United States of America | 2Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, United States of America | 3Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, United States of America

## Abstract

Nonadherence to antihypertensive medications is common. Mobile health (mHealth) based behavioral economic interventions may improve adherence, but remain largely untested, especially in vulnerable populations.

To test whether an mHealth incentive lottery would lower systolic blood pressure (SBP) and improve adherence.

BETTER-BP was a randomized trial conducted in 3 safety-net clinics in NYC. Eligible participants were adults with hypertension prescribed at least one antihypertensive medication, with SBP >140 mmHg, and poor self-reported adherence. In the intervention arm, an incentive lottery was administered via SMS messaging. All participants received passive adherence monitoring. The intervention lasted 6 months, with continued monitoring until 12 months. The primary clinical endpoint was change in SBP at 6 months. The primary process endpoint was adequate antihypertensive medication adherence (≥80% days adherent) from baseline to 6 months.

400 participants (265 intervention:135 control) were enrolled with median age 57 years, 60.5% women, 61.5% Hispanic, and 20.3% non-Hispanic Black. Over 70% had Medicaid or no insurance. At 6 months, intervention arm participants were twice as likely to achieve adequate adherence (71% vs. 34%, adjusted risk ratio [ARR] = 2.04, 95% CI 1.58, 2.63), but there was no significant change in mean SBP (−6.7 mmHg intervention vs. −5.8 mmHg control, P=0.62). From 6 to 12 months, adherence was similar (31% intervention vs. 26% control, ARR = 1.17, 95% CI 0.83, 1.65).

In a diverse safety-net population, the BETTER-BP intervention doubled the rate of adequate antihypertensive medication adherence but did not reduce SBP at 6 months.

## Abstract

In this randomized clinical trial of 400 adults with uncontrolled hypertension and low antihypertensive medication adherence, the proportion with adequate medication adherence doubled using a behavioral economics-based text incentive lottery over 6 months, but there was no significant difference in systolic blood pressure. After the lottery was removed from 6 to 12 months, adherence was similar between arms. The trial demonstrates that an incentive lottery can effectively improve antihypertensive medication adherence, but this did not translate to a reduction in systolic blood pressure, and the effect on adherence was not durable.

## Abstract

Behavioral Economics Trial to Enhance Regulation of Blood Pressure (BETTER-BP): Design and key findings.

## INTRODUCTION

Uncontrolled blood pressure (BP) continues to be a major public health problem.1 Even among those treated with antihypertensive medications in the U.S., at least one-third still have BP values above goal.1,2 Nonadherence to these medications is a major contributor to poor outcomes and remains a longstanding challenge despite decades of research.3,4 While patient education and counseling interventions have shown some benefit, 5,6 the most successful ones are typically resource-intensive and challenging to scale. Behavioral economics-based interventions provide an alternative approach that leverages innate human tendencies that are not always rational, including preference for immediate gains, inclination towards maintaining the status quo, and overestimating the likelihood of positive outcomes.7

One behavioral economics-based intervention in medicine is a “regret lottery” which encourages patients to pursue healthy behaviors by providing a financial gain if they perform a desired healthy behavior, enhanced by the desire to avoid regret over losing these potential financial incentives if the behavior is not completed.8,9 While some studies of these interventions have shown promise,8,9 others have been negative or demonstrated only modestly effective results.10–12 Further, whether these incentives translate to sustainable behavior change after the lottery is removed remains unclear.

Socioeconomically disadvantaged populations simultaneously experience the highest prevalence of hypertension, highest rates of adverse events attributable to hypertension (e.g. stroke), and the lowest levels of antihypertensive medication adherence.3,4 With few exceptions,13 regret lotteries for hypertension have not been evaluated in these populations. We therefore designed the randomized Behavioral Economics Trial To Enhance Regulation of Blood Pressure (BETTER-BP) with two aims: first, to test the effects of a lottery incentive on antihypertensive medication adherence; and second, to evaluate the impact of this lottery on SBP. We hypothesized that compared with control, the lottery would lead to improvements in medication adherence, as well as intermediate and long-term reductions in SBP.

## METHODS

### Trial Conduct and Oversight

A full description of BETTER-BP was published previously.14 The trial enrolled participants from 3 safety-net primary care clinics affiliated with a single medical school (NYU Grossman School of Medicine): Bellevue Hospital, Gouverneur Hospital, and NYU-Family Health Center Park Slope. Baseline study visits occurred between 7/14/2020 and 10/9/2024. The last 12-month follow-up visit occurred on 9/22/2025. The full trial protocol is provided as Supplement 1. We followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guideline for data analysis as well as manuscript preparation. The study operated through a single institutional review board (IRB) mechanism using the NYU Langone Health IRB, and all participants provided written informed consent. An independent data safety monitoring board (DSMB) met every 6 months to review enrollment and potential study-related adverse events. BETTER-BP employed several principles of a pragmatic trial, including broad eligibility, use of existing medications, and pairing of study visits with regular ambulatory follow-up care.15

### Trial Population

Eligibility criteria (eMethods, Supplement 2) included: age ≥18 years, clinical diagnosis of hypertension, on ≥1 antihypertensive medication, suboptimal BP control (≥1 outpatient SBP ≥140 within the past year), and poor self-reported adherence (<80% adherent with prescribed antihypertensive medication over the prior week). Patients were screened through the electronic health record based on having a scheduled ambulatory visit (primary care or cardiology) at one of the participating clinics. Those initially eligible were further screened by telephone for adherence based on a brief screening questionnaire developed by Voils et al.16 that ascertained antihypertensive adherence over the past 7 days. If they reported missing at least 2 doses of medication, they were then offered informed consent.

After enrollment of the first 269 participants, mean baseline SBP was estimated and noted to be lower (135 mmHg) than initially expected. After consultation and advisement by the funding agency and DSMB, a screen fail criterion was initiated such that participants with SBP <130 mmHg at the baseline visit would not undergo subsequent randomization. Effective 11/15/2022, the remaining 132 participants were enrolled with this criterion in place.

### Study Intervention

Participants were randomized in a 2:1 manner (intervention:control) (Figure 1 and Central Illustration). Unbalanced randomization was used to provide greater statistical power to understand trajectories of engagement in the intervention arm. Participants in both study arms received an electronic monitoring device (EMD) by AdhereTech (Summit, NJ) that had embedded cellular capabilities and registered a signal whenever the bottle was opened. A single antihypertensive medication class was chosen for the EMD, similar to other trials.17,18

Based on consultation with study physicians at participating sites prior to enrollment of the first participant, the following hierarchy was used: 1. ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker; 2. Calcium channel blocker; 3. Beta blocker; 4. Diuretic (including thiazide-type or aldosterone antagonist); 5. Other (e.g. clonidine). Further details are provided in described in the eMethods (Supplement 2).

For participants assigned to receive the study intervention, an incentive lottery was administered by Way to Health (Philadelphia, PA) a technology platform capable of delivering incentive lotteries with customizable features. The lottery was designed as a “combined lottery” with a low frequency chance of winning a large reward and a higher frequency chance of winning a small reward. Each participant was assigned a 2-digit number for the trial, and Way to Health randomly generated a 2-digit number daily. Participants received $50 if both digits matched (1 in 100 chance) or $5 if one digit matched (18 in 100 chance). The lottery also included a “regret” feature: patients whose number(s) matched were informed of the result whether or not they were adherent the previous day (i.e., opened the EMD bottle). Those who did not take their antihypertensive medication received a message indicating that had they been adherent, they would have won the prize (large or small based on one- or two-digit matches). Lottery results were delivered via Short Message Service (SMS) which was deliverable on any text-capable cellular phone (obviating the need for participants to own a smartphone). Sample text messages are shown in Figure 2, and a full list of messages is provided in eMethods, Supplement 2. The incentive lottery ran for 6 months; adherence was then monitored for an additional 6 months to examine durable effects. Participant winnings were calculated monthly and deposits were made on a rechargeable debit card (ClinCard) provided to study participants at the baseline visit. The lottery had an expected daily value (EDV) (calculated by multiplying the incentive amounts by the probabilities of winning) of $1.40, which was within range of other financial incentives described in a prior meta-analysis.8

Participants in the control group were instructed to use the AdhereTech EMD for the duration of the study and were passively monitored for medication adherence.

#### End Points

The primary clinical outcome was change in SBP from baseline to 6 months. SBP was measured in office, based on an average of 3 seated BP assessments obtained after a 5-minute rest period with an observer present, using an automated oscillometric device (Omron 907XL, Lake Forest, IL). BP cuff sizing and placement was performed by a research coordinator who received standardized training from a hypertension specialist (DS). Standardized measurements were obtained with the participant’s back supported, feet flat on the floor, and legs uncrossed.14

The null hypothesis was that change in SBP at 6 months in the intervention and control groups would not differ significantly. To provide adequate power to detect a significant difference of 10mmHg or greater between treatment arms, the trial was initially designed to enroll 435 participants with projected 20% dropout in each arm at 6 months, leaving 348 participants with evaluable endpoints. With a conservative standard error estimate of 28 mmHg,19 this provided approximately 88% power to detect a between-group difference of 10mmHg, using a two-sided, 0.05-level test. However, the trial faced several enrollment challenges, including delayed start due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the implementation of a “screen fail” criterion. In consultation with the NHLBI and DSMB, we implemented a new enrollment target of 401 participants which maintained 85% power to detect a 10 mmHg change in SBP between intervention and control arms assuming a 20% attrition rate.

The primary process outcome was adequate adherence defined as ≥80% of days adherent6 from baseline to 6 months. Adherence was calculated using the scheduling adherence metric, which is the proportion of days that a participant took their prescribed medication divided by the total number of days that they were expected to take medication in a given period.20

Secondary outcomes were change in SBP between 6 and 12 months, and adequate adherence from 6 to 12 months. As an exploratory outcome, we analyzed office diastolic BP (DBP) values obtained at baseline, 6, and 12 months. Safety endpoints included events that could be plausibly related to antihypertensive medication use, and included fall-related injury, hypotension, bradycardia, and renal or electrolyte abnormality.

#### Statistical Analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using R, version 4.2.2 (R Project for Statistical Computing). We used covariate-adjusted analysis for primary and secondary end points, adjusting for the prespecified prognostic covariates of age and study site.21 For analysis of the primary clinical endpoint (change in SBP), we used a linear regression model. We regressed 6-month SBP on a binary indicator of treatment group, with adjustment for baseline SBP, the stratification factor (enrollment site), and age. These covariates were chosen a priori given their plausible relationship with the study outcome. For the analysis of the primary process endpoint (adequate adherence), we used logistic regression with an indicator for treatment group, site and age and reported marginal risk-ratio and 95% CI to compare the proportion with adequate adherence between arms. We proceeded similarly for secondary endpoints, using linear regression for continuous outcomes and logistic regression for binary outcomes.

For the primary clinical endpoint, we reported point estimates and 95% CIs of the regression coefficient along with marginal means, and we tested for statistical significance using a 2-sided threshold of P < .05. We addressed the issue of multiple comparisons by implementing a hierarchical testing procedure in which the process outcome (adherence) would be formally tested only if the clinical endpoint (blood pressure) reached statistical significance. This is further described in Supplement 3.

For secondary endpoints, we reported point estimates and corresponding 95% CIs. We did not adjust for multiplicity, and thus did not conduct formal hypothesis tests for these endpoints. Outcomes at 12-month follow-up were modeled using a longitudinal mixed effects model and included fixed effects for randomization, time, their interaction and person level random effects to account for repeated measures (baseline, 6 months and 12 months).

The primary analysis was based on the intention-to-treat principle. Outcome analyses were conducted for all randomized participants (intention-to-treat sample) by imputing outcomes for those who did not complete the trial. For the primary clinical outcome at 6 months, we used multiple imputation with chained equations (eMethods in Supplement 2). Baseline variables, randomization status, all primary and secondary end points, and a priori identified subgroups were included in the imputation model. We performed 50 imputations and combined results from the imputed datasets using Rubin’s rule.22 We further assessed the primary end point in clinically relevant prespecified subgroups by treatment arm.

Investigators were blinded to the results until the database was locked. The full statistical analysis plan was finalized before unblinding the study outcomes and is provided as Supplement 3.

## RESULTS

### Patients

Among 8833 patients who were contacted, 1052 reported poor adherence, of whom 493 (46.9%) provided informed consent (Figure 3). There were 91 participants subsequently excluded due to meeting “screen fail” criteria (baseline SBP <130 mmHg), leaving 402 randomized. Among these 402, one participant was a duplicate enrollment, and one was deemed ineligible after enrollment, leaving a final intention-to-treat sample of 400.

Median age of the study population was 57 years (range 20 to 93 years), 242 (60.5%) were women, 246 (61.5%) were Hispanic, and 81 (20.3%) were non-Hispanic Black. Primary language was Spanish in 208 (52%) and English in 192 (48%) participants. More than 70% of participants had safety-net medical insurance or no insurance (148 [37.0%] Medicaid, 143 [35.8%] uninsured). The most common comorbidities were obesity (N=218, 54.5%) and diabetes (N=186, 46.5%). Mean baseline SBP was 138.8 (SD 19.1) mmHg and mean DBP was 82.3 (SD 13.2) mmHg.

At baseline, there were 265 participants randomized to intervention and 135 to control. The primary clinical endpoint assessment was completed by 235 intervention participants (88.7%) and 109 control participants (80.7%). Those with a missing endpoint at 6 months (N=56) were more likely to be male (44.6% vs. 38.7%), obese (60.7% vs. 53.5%), and report current tobacco use (16.1% vs. 9.9%), compared with those who had an endpoint measured. Missing endpoint data are further characterized in Tables S2 and S3.

There were 47% of participants who were taking more than one antihypertensive medication. The mean overall number of medications (antihypertensive and other) was 5.6. The most frequent class of medication chosen for the EMD was ACE inhibitor/ARB (N=230, 57.5%), followed by calcium channel blocker (N=105, 26.3%) (further described in Table S1). During the 6-month intervention period, study participants randomized to the lottery incentive arm received an average of $212 in lottery payouts (range $10 to $515).

### Efficacy

#### Primary Clinical Outcome

Mean baseline SBP was 137.9 (SD 19.3) mmHg in the intervention arm and 140.5 (18.6) mmHg in the control arm. At 6 months, estimated change in mean SBP from baseline was −6.7 (95%CI −8.9, −4.4) mmHg and −5.8 mmHg (95%CI −9.1, −2.4) mmHg in these arms respectively, which was not a statistically significant difference (P=0.62) (Figures 4A and 4B). As the hypothesis test for the primary clinical outcome was negative, no further significance testing was performed for other outcomes.

#### Primary Process Outcome

Using a threshold of ≥80% days adherent based on EMD usage, there were 187/265 (71%) participants in the intervention arm and 46/135 (34%) in the control arm who achieved adequate adherence between baseline and 6 months (adjusted risk ratio [ARR] = 2.04, 95% CI 1.58, 2.63) (Figure 5).

#### Secondary Outcomes

From 6 to 12 months, intervention vs. control change in mean SBP was −0.2 mmHg (95% CI −3.9, 3.5) mmHg and +3.6 (95% CI −1.8, 8.9) mmHg, respectively. During the same period, adherence among intervention arm participants approximated that of control arm participants; excluding the 5 participants who withdrew prior to 6 months, 82/261 (31%) of intervention arm participants achieved adequate adherence versus 35/134 (26%) in the control arm (ARR = 1.17, 95% CI 0.83, 1.65). The proportion of weekly days adherent over the entire 12-month study duration is shown in Figure 6.

#### Sensitivity Analyses

There were no appreciable differences when looking at subgroups defined by baseline SBP, or after implementing “screen fail” criteria. Specifically, when stratified by baseline SBP, the estimated difference in the primary clinical endpoint did not vary by baseline SBP status (baseline SBP < 140 mm Hg: difference between arms in estimated 6-month SBP change (95% CI) = −0.71 (−5.08, 3.65); baseline SBP ≥ 140 mm Hg: difference between arms in the estimated 6-month SBP change (95% CI) = −0.83 (−6.55, 4.89)). There was also no difference in this endpoint before and after implementation of the “screen fail” criteria whereby participants with baseline SBP <130 mmHg were excluded (before implementation: difference between arms in estimated 6-month SBP change (95% CI) = −1.03 (−5.38, 3.32); after implementation: difference between arms in estimated 6-month SBP change (95% CI) = −0.46 (−6.27, 5.34)).

### Treatment effect heterogeneity

Change in mean SBP by prespecified clinically relevant subgroups is shown in Figure S1. Comparing intervention vs. control participants, there were no observed differences based on confidence intervals among subgroups of race, age, comorbidity burden, health status, or number of medications.

### Exploratory analyses

Mean (SD) study DBP at baseline was 82.1 (13.1) mmHg in the intervention arm and 82.9 (13.6) mmHg in the control arm. At 6-month follow-up, estimated change in mean DBP from baseline was −3.6 (95%CI −5.7, 0.1) mmHg and −2.8 (95%CI −5.6, −1.6) mmHg in these arms respectively. From 6 to 12 months, estimated change in mean DBP was −0.4 (95%CI −2.5, 1.7) mmHg and 1.4 (95%CI −1.7, 4.5) mmHg, respectively (Figure S2).

### Safety

There were no signals of increased harm for serious adverse events (hospitalization or death) with the study intervention; the rates of these events were similar in the intervention arm (30/265, 11.3%) and control arm (14/135, 10.4%) (Table S4). We also collected non-serious events that may be plausibly related to antihypertensive medication taking (bradycardia, hypotension, renal/electrolyte abnormalities, minor fall-related injuries, syncope). There was a higher rate of minor fall-related injuries in the intervention vs. control arm (9/265, 3.4% vs. 0/135, 0%) as well as episodes of hypotension (19/265, 7.2% vs. 6/135, 4.4%). Rates of bradycardia (2/265, 0.8% vs. 0/135, 0.0%), renal/electrolyte abnormalities (26/265, 9.8% vs. 14/135, 10.4%), and syncope (4/265, 1.5% vs. 1/135, 0.7%) were relatively similar between intervention vs. control arms.

## DISCUSSION

Our study had several key findings: first, the incentive lottery doubled adequate antihypertensive medication adherence compared with the control arm, from 34% to 71%, between baseline and 6 months. Second, despite this improvement, there was no evidence of an effect of the incentive lottery on the primary endpoint of SBP at 6 months. Third, the lottery did not lead to durable effect on adherence after its removal. And finally, there was no meaningful change in SBP after the lottery was removed.

We note that our effect size for adherence is larger than a number of other prior interventions for cardiovascular medications, including antihypertensive therapies,23–25 yet this still failed to translate into a difference in SBP at 6 months. There are several potential explanations for this finding (Figure 7). First, as a pragmatic trial, we chose a single medication for the EMD (for purposes of both minimizing EMD-related costs and to avoid complexity24), but 47% of study participants were prescribed more than one antihypertensive medication at baseline. Increased adherence with a single antihypertensive medication may have failed to translate to other non-selected antihypertensive medications in this subgroup, leading to suboptimal BP reduction. Second, our primary endpoint relied on standardized BP measurements at in-person visits.26,27 Participants in both arms may have taken their antihypertensive medications for several days in anticipation of the 6-month study visit. Clinical trials are increasingly including home-based BP assessments, but this was not performed in BETTER-BP. Third, we used EMD-monitored adherence, and it remains possible that some intervention arm participants opened the EMD on a regular basis in order to potentially receive the lottery incentive, but did not actually take the medication. Fourth, mean baseline SBP in the study sample was 138.8 mmHg, which – although similar to several prior hypertension trials28,29 – provided limited room for improvement in the intervention arm compared with control. Finally, increasing adherence alone for several days per week, as was observed among our intervention participants, may be an insufficient strategy to lower SBP further; alternative strategies (e.g. therapeutic intensification) may be higher yield.

There are several other important implications to our work. By design, BETTER-BP recruited study participants from a socioeconomically disadvantaged population, with the majority having either safety-net or no health insurance. These patients typically have higher rates of adverse hypertension-related sequelae, lower rates of medication adherence, and have not been included in many behavioral economics trials.1,4,30 BETTER-BP demonstrated the feasibility of conducting a complex, technology-driven randomized trial in this population. This achievement is notable given the competing structural barriers that undermine clinical trial participation in health disparity populations such as limited digital access and literacy, competing life demands, and medical mistrust. BETTER-BP challenges the notion that these populations are “hard to reach” by showing that high consent and engagement rates are possible when clinical trials and digital health interventions are explicitly designed with equity and inclusivity at their core.31 For example, in order to overcome language barriers we employed an entirely bilingual team of research coordinators. We also coordinated study visits on the same day as existing medical appointments whenever possible, in recognition of challenges with transportation. While socioeconomically disadvantaged populations often face competing structural barriers that undermine clinical trial participation, our high consent and retention rates suggest that the SMS based regret lottery intervention was able to maintain high engagement even up to 12 months.

Another notable finding of BETTER-BP is the failure of initial increased adherence to translate into sustained adherence once the lottery incentive was removed. The trial was originally designed as a novel approach to a longstanding problem; according to a recent scientific statement from the American Heart Association, the most successful adherence interventions have typically been multicomponent programs that are costly and personnel-intensive which has limited their ability to impact broad populations of patients.6 In this context, BETTER-BP employed the theory that small automated financial incentives, provided through behavioral economics, would serve as a “nudge” to strengthen intrinsic motivation over time.32 This approach is appealing as short term financial incentives have the potential to be deployed at scale, in contrast with either long-term financial incentives or more personnel-intensive interventions that are considerably more costly. However, failure of a sustainable effect on adherence in BETTER-BP adds to a growing literature of cardiovascular clinical trials using behavioral economics that have similarly failed to show a sustained benefit after the end of the intervention,9,23,33 and a critical reexamining of such approaches may be warranted. Pairing short-term financial incentives with durable cost-effective mHealth behavioral strategies for long-term engagement (e.g. chatbots using generative artificial intelligence34) may be one future direction, but require prospective trials. A second direction may be employing behavioral economics in time-limited medication adherence scenarios (for example, antibiotic therapy) where durable effects are not required. While most cardiovascular medications require long-term adherence over years, behavioral economics may also have a role in time-limited medication scenarios such as dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary revascularization.

### Limitations

Our findings must be interpreted in the context of our study design. First, our study focused on a single mechanism (medication nonadherence) and other interventions (e.g. escalation in therapy) may have improved BP control. Second, enrollment was based on a single office SBP value >140 mmHg within the past year, coupled with self-reported nonadherence. While more stringent criteria could have been used (e.g. average of multiple high BP readings), our aim was to conduct a pragmatic trial that was broadly inclusive. Additionally, decisions in clinical practice are often made based on a single high office SBP. Third, we did not formally measure health literacy in our population, which may have been helpful in further analyzing treatment effect heterogeneity. Fourth, biochemical adherence testing is a “gold standard” alternative to EMDs,35 but we did not use this given cost and pragmatic concerns. If this had been used on a subset of trial participants, it may have better elucidated the accuracy of EMD use in this population. Finally, our trial was conducted in an urban environment with high cellular connectivity, and may be difficult to implement in areas with more limited access.

## Conclusion

BETTER-BP demonstrated that a large-scale technology-enabled randomized trial could be successfully implemented in safety-net clinics that serve a diverse population, where the burden of hypertension sequelae is particularly high. While the behavioral economics-based lottery doubled the rate of adequate medication adherence from baseline to 6 months, this did not translate to a reduction in SBP compared with control, and increased adherence was not sustained after the lottery was removed. This distinction between changing behavior and changing physiology helps to define the boundary of what short-term financial incentives are able to achieve in the management of chronic disease.
